note: POST-HOC, EXPLORATORY (in neither ANALYSIS_PLAN.md nor its addendum). Seven matched merge system prompts over the frozen 320-item discrimination bank. P1-P6 differ from the shipped prompt in exactly one clause, the one that specifies how to weigh the signals. P4 and P5 are the controls for the under-specification objection: they raise the standing-rule question WITHOUT naming qualifying categories or indicating which items are which, where P3 asserts constraint primacy and enumerates categories. P6 is ELICITED chain-of-thought, not a reasoning-mode model, to which we have no API access. P0 is the one condition that is NOT a one-clause diff: the shipped prompt names the metadata in three places (the input description, the trust-ordering clause, the abstention instruction) and P0 replaces all three, so it mentions no metadata, no trust ordering and no standing rule at all. The branch payloads still carry source and confidence, since those are the data rather than the prompt; P0 tests only whether being TOLD about them is what produces the field-reading. Note P0's lower coverage: an unprimed merger abstains more, so read took_update_rate and wrong_commit_rate alongside the accuracies. Scenario construction, arms and scoring are imported from run_discrimination_experiment.py so the items match the preregistered run exactly and P1 is cache-served. Intervals resample template families.

prompt_texts.P1_shipped: You are reconciling two independently-updated branches of an agent's memory that diverged from a common ancestor while disconnected from each other. For each conflicting (entity, predicate) key, you are given the common ancestor's value (if any) and each branch's current value, source, and confidence. 'source' is how that update was recorded: "user" means the user explicitly stated or corrected it; "inference" means the agent inferred or guessed it; "observation" means the agent observed it indirectly. Resolve each conflict using whatever signal actually distinguishes the two updates — e.g. a user-sourced, higher-confidence update is ordinarily more trustworthy than an inferred, lower-confidence one; the ancestor value can indicate which branch's update is more likely a genuine correction vs. a stale duplicate. Do NOT use timestamps to decide, even if you can infer relative recency — two branches that were disconnected from each other have no shared clock, so 'later' does not mean 'more correct' here. If source, confidence, and ancestor context give no real basis to prefer one branch over the other (e.g. both are equally plausible, equally-sourced preference changes), explicitly flag it as unresolvable rather than guessing.
prompt_texts.P4_unmarked_rule: You are reconciling two independently-updated branches of an agent's memory that diverged from a common ancestor while disconnected from each other. For each conflicting (entity, predicate) key, you are given the common ancestor's value (if any) and each branch's current value, source, and confidence. 'source' is how that update was recorded: "user" means the user explicitly stated or corrected it; "inference" means the agent inferred or guessed it; "observation" means the agent observed it indirectly. Resolve each conflict in two steps. First, decide for yourself what kind of entry the ancestor value is: a standing commitment that remains in force until it is explicitly withdrawn, or an ordinary value that a later, better update may legitimately replace. Then decide the conflict accordingly. If it is a standing commitment and one branch's value is incompatible with it, keep the compatible value even if the incompatible branch is user-sourced or carries higher confidence. If it is an ordinary value, let source and confidence decide, preferring a user-sourced, higher-confidence update over an inferred, lower-confidence one. Do NOT use timestamps to decide, even if you can infer relative recency — two branches that were disconnected from each other have no shared clock, so 'later' does not mean 'more correct' here. If source, confidence, and ancestor context give no real basis to prefer one branch over the other (e.g. both are equally plausible, equally-sourced preference changes), explicitly flag it as unresolvable rather than guessing.
